title: House parties after excursions and Cap's last night
summary: His home filled on Sundays after excursion trains, and he recalls Cap going out to jam the night before he died.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: That's right. When it hits a family, it really does hit it. And, uh, I mean, we didn't have any way of word about getting this one to play with us, about one to play because everybody just wanted to, uh, play. Not like Jeanette. Jeanette, sweetest she could be. You didn't have to beg her to come play a number on the piano. Or you have to say, Jeanette, do you feel like playing? Oh, she was right there ready. And at my house, well, on a Saturday, I mean on a Sunday evenings, we would have what you call, at my house, well, the elder people knew what houses that you were going to after excursion leave. You see, they used to have an excursion, we'd leave from over here on a Sunday morning, and bring so many people over the lake. And at six o'clock in the evening, that excursion was coming back over here. You see, well, some people would come and spend the whole day. They had friends and different ones and all like that. Well, I was in a musical family. And at that time, like the elder people, they would tell their daughters, you could go by old man John Hander's house, but I don't want you to go any further. My daddy was well respected, just like people talk now that, uh, they had colored policemen and this and that. When I was around 12 and 14 years old, he used to put a badge on my daddy and tell him to go out there and arrest anybody. Yeah. Because he was a real guy, well respected, and he knew how to take care of himself. And, uh, so, our house would be packed like that. Jeanette Bisping and Bapin, I mean, as you said, I was packed up at my house. That's a wonderful way to roll up. We had a piano, and we had, uh, all kind of records and had a great big old, uh, draft of phone. Well, there wasn't nothing doing wrong. There wasn't nothing there to do because we all was the same kind of, you know, we all just went there, come back for a good time. That's all we had. And, uh, it was wonderful. And everybody thought they knew how to play a little something. They were there. And that's what made a lot of good musicians over the lake because they used to come there and listen to different ones and they used to have to teach each other. And that's what made so many others so great. And I like this little Joe, Joseph Jackson, he belonged to the union here. Because Cap used to bring him over here. And, uh, played with a lot of numbers, you know, a lot of jobs over here. And then, if he get a job right now, a good job, he'll call for me. So, that's the night you should go and play with him a lot of times. And Cap used to get a lot of jobs over the lake. And, uh, a lot of times Cap would tell him, he said, I got to play at the preservation hall tonight. And I'd call for him up sheep and explain to him, you know, to try to get somebody else to say, because these are my home folks and he said, and they have a big dance tonight. And he said, now at the last minute, he come and ask me to play with this band. He was kicking. Do you know the night before Cap, uh, the morning before Cap died? They worried Cap about dancing teenagers. And, uh, Cap was feeling good. And they kept worrying Cap to come by the PC Club to, uh, jam with.

Peter Clayton. Oh. Peter Clayton Club over the past. And Cap, he just preached himself. And he went on out there and, uh, played a few numbers with him and he come on back home. But he, uh, his wife said he didn't feel like going. But he never did, he never did.
He didn't want to turn him down. Turned anybody down.
He just get up and go anywhere. So, it was just one of those things. He said, get a kick out of my dad everywhere he'd go. I had to go. Take me with him everywhere.
